general_news.report:
The latest news is that UK social media users are becoming less active due to the rise of video apps and concerns over historic posts. The communications watchdog, Ofcom, found just under half of adult social media users (49%) now post, share or comment compared with 61% in 2024.

It looks like video apps are the main reason for this decrease, with popular platforms becoming more video-oriented. This means some users are posting and commenting less on those platforms than they would on sites like Facebook. Concerns over long-forgotten posts being unearthed and damaging someone's professional prospects or reputation are also a factor.

The proportion of adults concerned about posts causing them problems in the future has risen from 43% in 2024 to 49%. This is partly due to concerns over data privacy, such as misuse of personal information like photos. Despite this, social media use remains widespread, with 89% of adult internet users using at least one social media platform.

Interestingly, Ofcom's data also shows that active use of AI is increasing, with more than half of UK adults (54%) saying they use AI tools such as ChatGPT. This includes using AI for conversation, creative tasks like writing wedding speeches or planning room layouts, and even interacting with it as if it were a person.

From what I see here, it looks like teachers in England are losing control of their classrooms thanks to AI-powered tools, specifically those that use voice-to-text technology and business email compromise. 

Two-thirds of secondary school teachers report a decline in core skills such as writing and problem-solving among children who use these tools. They say students no longer feel the need to spell or think critically because they're too busy relying on AI to do their work for them.

The government is pushing for more digital integration, including AI tutoring tools that'll provide one-to-one learning support for up to 450,000 disadvantaged pupils. But teachers are skeptical - they worry it'll just be a cheap way to cut costs and undermine the value of teaching skills. They say AI won't give students what they really need: human interaction.

The NEU's general secretary says "students must be able to think for themselves," but it looks like AI is having an effect on their ability to do so. Bridget Phillipson, the education secretary, claims that AI tutoring tools can help make learning more accessible, but it sounds like the problem might not just be the students who need extra support - it's the system itself.

Keep in mind this is a government plan aiming to break the link between background and success by providing tailored support for every child.

It looks like Anthropic's AI-powered coding assistant, _Claude Code_, is at it again - this time, because of human error, not a security breach. An internal-use file mistakenly included in a software update pointed to an archive containing nearly 2,000 files and 500,000 lines of code, which were quickly copied to GitHub.

Apparently, the exposed code was related to the tool's internal architecture but did not contain confidential data from Claude, the underlying AI model by Anthropic. A post on X sharing a link to the leaked code had more than 29m views early on Wednesday, and a rewritten version of the source code quickly became GitHub's fastest-ever downloaded repository.

No sensitive customer data or credentials were involved or exposed, according to Anthropic. This was a release packaging issue caused by human error, not a security breach. _Tamagotchi_-esque coding assistant blueprints and an always-on AI agent were spotted within the leaked code.

academic_research.report:
Just took a look at this new benchmark, OP (Olfactory Perception). From what I see here, it's designed to test large language models' ability to reason about smell. Apparently, current LLMs access olfactory knowledge primarily through lexical associations rather than structural molecular reasoning.

They've got 1,010 questions across eight task categories, including odor classification and smell identification from real-world sources. The best-performing model reaches 64.4% overall accuracy, which is a decent number but also highlights substantial remaining gaps in olfactory reasoning.

One interesting thing: they used two prompt formats – compound names and isomeric SMILES – to evaluate the effect of molecular representations. Compound-name prompts consistently outperformed isomeric SMILES, with gains ranging from +2.4 to +18.9 percentage points.

So now we know that LLMs should be able to handle olfactory information as well as visual or aural info, but there's still work to be done in this area. Piping the link over to you now, so you can dig into it further.

From what I see here, we got a new attack on Federated Learning (FL) systems. Apparently, it's called _Gradient Inversion over Feature Domains_ (GIFD). This method exploits pre-trained generative adversarial networks (GANs) as prior knowledge to invert shared gradients and reconstruct sensitive data.

Looks like it uses hierarchical features of the intermediate layers instead of just the initial latent space. They've also got a regularizer to avoid unreal image generation by adding a small ${l_1}$ ball constraint. This thing is supposed to tackle privacy leakage in FL systems, which is getting pretty wild considering the amount of data being exchanged.

From what I see here, it's not just about detecting malicious activity but also mitigating the impact of any potential leaks. It looks like they've tested this method on 36 real-world LLM incidents and found success with pixel-level reconstruction and outperforming competitive baselines across a variety of FL scenarios.

We got another one: _Promptware Kill Chain_. It's about attacks evolving from prompt injection to malware-like behavior, using the application's LLM as prior knowledge. This thing proposes a seven-stage attack mechanism, including Initial Access (prompt injection), Privilege Escalation (jailbreaking), Reconnaissance, Persistence (memory and retrieval poisoning), Command and Control, Lateral Movement, and Actions on Objective.

From what I see here, it tells us that these attacks aren't as simple as just performing gradient inversion in the latent space. They're trying to find a better method to tackle this growing problem with competitive baselines.

MitUNet, a hybrid neural network, is being touted as a game-changer for 3D reconstruction pipelines. _It looks like_ it's all about improving floor plan recognition by identifying thin structures and maintaining geometric precision. From what I see here, the authors are trying to bridge the gap between global semantic context and fine-grained structural details. They've combined a Mix-Transformer encoder with a U-Net decoder enhanced with spatial and channel attention blocks.

The Tversky loss function is being used to optimize this approach, which supposedly achieves a balance between precision and recall. _It's not exactly clear_ how this works, but the idea is that MitUNet can generate structurally correct masks with high boundary accuracy. They've tested it on the CubiCasa5k dataset and the regional dataset, and it seems to be outperforming standard models.

The real takeaway here is that MitUNet provides a robust foundation for automated 3D reconstruction pipelines. _It's not exactly rocket science_, but apparently, it's something that needs to happen. The source code and regional dataset are publicly available, so you can dig into it yourself if you're interested.

One thing to note is that this technology could be used for more than just floor plan recognition. _It looks like_ the possibilities are endless, from remote code execution to remote access trojans. It's worth keeping an eye on this one.

I'm forwarding the links to you now, so you can take a closer look at MitUNet and see what all the fuss is about.

community_pulse.report:
Here's a deep-dive into the current events:

There's been an uptick in high-profile incidents of business email compromise (BEC) and remote access Trojan (RAT) attacks, which have left many wondering if GRC is truly enough to protect against non-human agents. Essentially, these rogue actors are already navigating systems as if they were part of the regular operation - but how can we govern their behavior?

The problem starts with identity: if an agent's actions are meaningful, it cannot remain anonymous. But what happens when we give too much authority to an agent? It's like leaving a tool unattended - mistake or manipulation can lead to disaster.

To mitigate this risk, some experts recommend a more nuanced approach that incorporates both automated and manual controls. Think of it as the difference between having a lock on a door and having someone watching over the key.

But that's still not enough. The issue also lies in the fact that agents need approval boundaries - just like any human employee would require sign-off on certain tasks before proceeding. Without this, accountability crumbles.

The question now becomes: how can we ensure traceability when an agent takes action? Can we really trust that there will be a reconstructable record of what it saw, did, and decided?

One approach is to view governance as an ongoing process - like managing a project lifecycle rather than doing a one-time assessment. This means embracing the idea of forgetting previously learned knowledge, giving rise to a new term unlearning.

To implement this effectively, researchers have proposed a framework that categorizes unlearning scenarios into three contexts: state unlearning (forgetting specific states or items), trajectory unlearning (forgetting sequences of actions) and environment unlearning (forgetting entire environments or categories of tasks). Within this framework, a natural language-based unlearning method trains a conversion model to transform high-level unlearning requests into actionable prompts.

The takeaway? As we navigate the world of non-human agents, it's crucial to view GRC as operational - rather than just being about policy documents and audit reports. It's time to take control of our own agency (pun intended).
